newsitem.title: USA: Motorola's twin woes seen as unique.
newsitem.headline: Motorola's twin woes seen as unique.

text.p: Motorola Inc's warning of weaker profits in the third quarter reveals at least as much about its ongoing problems as dual chip/cell phone maker as widespread weakness in its respective markets.
As a hybrid, Motorola has suffered a cruel simultaneous sales downturn in both its main product lines.
Making matters worse, Motorola's woes are apparently intensifying even as some of its rivals are showing signs of recovering from sharp industrywide market corrections, analysts said.

That Motorola's woes are intensifying while rivals such as Intel Corp in chips and Nokia AB in cell phones are emerging from tough markets, highlights the company-specific issues afflicting it, analysts said.
"Motorola tends to be a more broad line supplier of commodity-type products," said Mark Edelstone, semiconductor analyst at Prudential Securities.
"For companies with proprietary products, like Intel, the correction is already coming to an end," Edelstone said.
Indeed, August's semiconductor book-to-bill index, released yesterday, improved to 0.90 from July's 0.86.
The report from the Semiconductor Industry Association showed orders up month-over-month for the first time all year.
Analysts said the rise, which took place during what is generally the industry's weakest month, was a positive sign and may signal an upturn is near.
Separately, the chief economist at Texas Instruments said the semiconductor industry could see a fourth-quarter upturn .

In discussing its profit warning, Motorola told analysts on a conference call third quarter earnings could fall 25 percent or more compared to the second quarter, when it earned $0.54 per share. It said its Q3 book-to-bill would remain weak.

The warning could have been quite troubling for shareholders in Nokia and Swedish mobile telecoms outfit Ericsson, whose shares have tended to trade somewhat in tandem with each other because their cell phone markets commingle so directly.
However, despite Motorola's tumble ahead of the market opening by as much as four points to 46-3/4, U.S.-listed shares in Nokia fell no more than 3/4 in early trade.
Motorola later recovered to 49, off 1-5/8 on the day. Meanwhile, by mid-morning, Nokia fell just 1/4 to 41 and Ericsson shares were off a mere 1/8 to 23-7/8.
